title: The Story of Hanuman
note_html:
॥ॐ॥

मनोजवं मारुततुल्यवेगं जितेन्द्रियं बुद्धिमतां वरिष्ठम्।
वातात्मजं वानरयूथमुख्यं श्रीरामदूतं शरणं प्रपद्ये॥

Why this collection:

Sundarakanda is one of the most beloved sections of the Valmiki Ramayana. It narrates the heroic journey of Hanuman as he crosses the ocean, discovers Sita in Lanka, delivers Rama's message, consoles her in her time of distress, and returns with news of her whereabouts. More than a tale of adventure and courage, Sundarakanda is a profound spiritual journey that illustrates devotion, faith, perseverance, wisdom, and selfless service.

Among all the characters of the Ramayana, Hanuman stands as the perfect embodiment of strength guided by humility, power tempered by wisdom, and unwavering devotion to Rama.

I chose to undertake this project because Sundarakanda has long held a special place in my heart. In particular, the events leading up to Hanuman's leap across the ocean serve as a powerful reminder that we often possess far greater strength than we realize. Just as Jambavan helped Hanuman rediscover his hidden potential, we too are blessed at times with guides, teachers, friends, or well-wishers who encourage us when we face seemingly impossible challenges.

By including selected sargas from Kishkindhakanda and Yuddhakanda alongside Sundarakanda, I hope to present a more complete picture of Hanuman's inspiring journey—from the awakening of his confidence, to his heroic service in Lanka, and finally to his selfless efforts in service of Rama. My prayer is that the study and recitation of these sacred verses may inspire the same faith, courage, devotion, and determination in everyone who reads them.

Sargas 66 and 67 of Kishkindhakanda

Before Hanuman prepares to leap across the ocean in search of Sita, the vanaras are overcome with despair. Faced with what appears to be an impossible task, they lose hope of success. Hanuman himself remains unaware of the immense strength and potential that lie dormant within him. At this crucial moment, in Sarga 66, Jambavan steps forward and reminds him of his true nature, his divine gifts, and his extraordinary capabilities.

In Sarga 67, Hanuman awakens to his own strength. His confidence is restored, his doubts disappear, and he finds the courage to undertake the seemingly impossible journey across the vast ocean.

We encounter similar moments in our own lives. There are times when challenges appear insurmountable and we feel that all hope is lost. Yet, by the grace of the divine, we are sometimes blessed with someone who believes in us, encourages us, and helps us rediscover the strength that was within us all along. With renewed confidence and faith, we find the courage to face our difficulties and overcome them.

It is for this reason that I have chosen to include these two sargas from Kishkindhakanda as a prelude to Sundarakanda. They beautifully set the stage for Hanuman's extraordinary journey and remind us of the transformative power of faith, encouragement, and self-discovery.

Just as Hanuman successfully fulfilled the mission entrusted to him by Rama, may he bless us with the strength, courage, devotion, and determination to fulfil the duties and responsibilities entrusted to us in our own lives.

The Sanjivani Episodes

Sarga 74 of Yuddhakanda is another important chapter in Hanuman's story. During the great war, when Lakshmana and many of the vanara heroes are struck down by Indrajit's powerful weapons, Hanuman brings the Sanjivani-bearing mountain to restore them and enable Rama's mission to continue. Hanuman's glorious service to Rama cannot be fully appreciated without this episode.

Later, in Sarga 101 of Yuddhakanda, when Lakshmana is once again grievously wounded in battle, Hanuman undertakes the same heroic mission and brings the Sanjivani-bearing mountain once more. These episodes represent some of the finest moments in Hanuman's life, where he places the welfare of Rama, Lakshmana, and the vanara army above everything else. They demonstrate not only his extraordinary power but also his unwavering devotion and selfless service to Rama.

I chose to include these episodes because Hanuman's story does not end with the discovery of Sita in Lanka. His devotion to Rama continues to manifest itself through ever-greater acts of courage, strength, and sacrifice. For Sarga 101, however, I have included only those shlokas that describe Hanuman's journey to bring the mountain, in order to maintain the focus on Hanuman.

The Coronation of Rama

I have also included the coronation of Rama as the concluding chapter of this collection. Every great journey deserves a fitting conclusion, and Hanuman's story finds its fulfilment in Rama's victory and return to Ayodhya. The coronation marks the triumph of dharma, the successful completion of Rama's mission, and the joyous culmination of all the efforts and sacrifices made by Hanuman and countless others in Rama's service.

It therefore serves as a natural and auspicious ending to The Story of Hanuman, reminding us that sincere devotion and selfless service ultimately lead to the victory of righteousness and the fulfilment of the Divine Will.

॥ जय श्री हनुमान् ॥
॥ सर्वं श्री कृष्णार्पणमस्तु ॥

title: Narayaneeyam
note_html:
A Short Summary

Narayaneeyam is a devotional Sanskrit poem of 1,036 verses divided into 100 dashakas (cantos), composed by Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri in the late 16th century. It is a condensed retelling of the Shrimad Bhagavatam, especially emphasizing devotion (bhakti) to Lord Krishna as the Supreme Being.

The work begins by describing the supreme, transcendental nature of Narayana, the creation of the universe, and the various incarnations of Vishnu. It then narrates the lives of great devotees and sages before devoting nearly half the work to Krishna's life, from His birth, childhood sports in Gokula and Vrindavana, lifting Govardhana, subduing various asuras, the Rasa-lila, His life in Mathura and Dwaraka, and many episodes from the Tenth Canto of the Bhagavatam.

Throughout the poem, Bhattathiri interweaves philosophical teachings of Vedanta with intense devotion, presenting Krishna as both the Supreme Brahman and the most lovable personal deity. The final dasakas culminate in a magnificent meditation on the beautiful form of Guruvayurappan (Krishna of Guruvayoor), concluding with the poet's heartfelt prayer for devotion, spiritual liberation, and freedom from disease.

Traditionally, the Narayaneeyam is recited as an act of devotion, and it is especially revered at the Guruvayoor Temple in Kerala. According to tradition, Bhattathiri composed it while suffering from severe rheumatism, offering one dashaka each day to Lord Guruvayurappan, and is believed to have regained his health upon completing the hundredth dashaka.

Story of how Guruvayoor came to be

According to tradition, at the end of Dvapara Yuga, when Dwaraka was about to be submerged, Uddhava was inconsolable, saying that if Krishna goes away, who will guide the world. Then Krishna asks Uddhava to take the sacred idol of Lord Vishnu that had been worshipped in Vaikuntha and later by Vasudeva and Krishna Himself. Krishna entrusted the idol to Brihaspati (Guru), the preceptor of the Devas, asking him to find a suitable place in the South and establish it for worship.

Guru, accompanied by his disciple Vayu, the Lord of Winds, journeyed southward and, guided by Lord Parasurama, reached a beautiful, verdant spot beside a lotus-filled lake. There they installed the sacred idol. The place came to be known as Guruvayoor, combining the names of Guru and Vayu. “Oor” means city. Because the deity came from Dwaraka and continued the worship of Lord Krishna, Guruvayoor is revered as the "Dwaraka of the South."

title: Eclectic Collection
note_html:
Kavyakusumanjali — An Offering of Flowers from the Garden of Sanskrit Poetry.

Sanskrit literature is an immense ocean of poetic beauty, wisdom and imagination. Scattered across its mahakavyas and other great works are countless passages that linger in the mind — vivid descriptions of nature, tender moments of human emotion, episodes of nobility and devotion, and reflections on the many shades of life.

This collection is an attempt to gather some of these exquisite passages into a single garland. It brings together selected sargas and episodes from different works and poets: Rama's lyrical evocation of the rainy season and the beauty of autumn in the Kishkindha Kanda; Dileepa's encounter with Nandini in Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha; and many such other jewels drawn from the rich treasury of Sanskrit poetry.

The selections are eclectic, guided not by chronology or completeness, but by an appreciation of literary excellence, poetic charm and the enduring beauty of expression. Each piece is intended to stand on its own, while together they offer a glimpse into the extraordinary range and splendour of the Sanskrit literary tradition.

It is, in essence, a personal anthology — a garland woven from the finest flowers of Sanskrit kavya.
